interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on one plot. A capacitor C, charged to 12 V, discharges through a resistor R, drawn small beside the plot. Voltage runs up the side, from 0 to 12 V. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 10 s. The opening parts are R = 20 kΩ and C = 100 µF, so RC = 2 s. The current leaving the capacitor is v ÷ R. Since i = C dv/dt, the rule is dv/dt = −v ÷ RC. So the voltage falls at a rate in proportion to what is left: 6 V a second at 12 V, 3 V a second at 6 V. A shaded window of fixed width sits on the curve. Readouts show the voltage at its start, the voltage at its end, and end ÷ start. A rate arrow at each end of the window shows the rule's slope there, −v ÷ RC, so the end arrow is always shallower than the start arrow by the same ratio. Because the rate is always the same share of the voltage, every window of one width keeps the same share. A 1 s window reads e^(−1/2), which is 0.607. A switch flips the sign to dy/dt = +y ÷ 2, from 1, over 0 to 4 s on its own scale. Then a 1 s window multiplies by 1.649 wherever it sits. On a phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. Screen by screen: 1 shows the circuit and the rule, with rate arrows on the curve at 12 V and 6 V. 2 asks the rate at 3 V: −1.5 V a second, −6 V a second or +1.5 V a second. 3 lets you drag the 1 s window. Wherever it sits, end ÷ start reads 0.607, from 12 V to 7.28 V or from 2.68 V to 1.62 V. The sign switch shows growth by 1.649 in every 1 s. 4 puts the window at 3 s and asks what end ÷ start reads: the same 0.607, smaller because it is nearer zero, or larger because the curve is flatter. 5 separates the rule. The v terms slide to the left side and the t terms to the right: dv ÷ v = −dt ÷ RC. 6 asks which line separates dN/dt = −λN: dN ÷ N = −λ dt, dN = −λN dt, or N dN = −λ dt. 7 integrates both sides to ln v = −t ÷ RC + c, then v = A e^(−t/RC). A family of curves for different A fans out, and the start at 12 V picks one, v = 12 e^(−t/2). 8 asks which curve starts at 9 V with τ = 3 s: v = 9 e^(−t/3), v = e^(−t/3) or v = 9 e^(−3t). A wrong pick is drawn so you can see its start or its pace is wrong. 9 puts the answer back into the rule. A rider slides along 12 e^(−t/2) with two readouts, the curve's slope and −v ÷ 2. They agree everywhere: at 2 s both read −2.21 V a second. 10 asks which rule y = 5 e^(−2t) solves: dy/dt = −2y, dy/dt = −y ÷ 2 or dy/dt = −10. 11 sets the window to one RC wide, and end ÷ start reads 0.368. A straight tangent leaves the start at the starting rate, −6 V a second, and reaches zero at 2 s. The curve is still at 4.41 V there. R and C sliders appear, R from 10 to 40 kΩ and C from 50 to 150 µF. They stretch the curve, the tangent and the window together, so the window still reads 0.368 and the tangent still lands at one RC. 12 and 13 mix it all. 12 takes a coil of 0.5 H carrying 2.4 A whose current dies round a loop through 10 Ω, and asks the current after 0.05 s: 0.883 A, 0 A or 1.52 A. 13 takes dy/dt = +y ÷ 5 from 100 and asks the value after 5 s: about 272, 200 or 36.8. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: The parts are ideal. A real capacitor leaks a little through itself, and a real resistor warms and changes slightly. The curve is drawn at once, not in real time. Near 10 s it looks as if it touches zero, but by this rule it never quite does. The voltages, resistances and capacitances are example values. The growth switch has no units, and no real quantity can grow this way for ever.

explain.text:
When a quantity falls at a rate in proportion to what is left, it loses the same fraction in every equal stretch of time. Its curve is y = A e^(−t/τ), and the rule itself leads there. Take a capacitor charged to v volts, discharging through a resistor R. By Ohm's law the current leaving it is v ÷ R. You know i = C dv/dt. That current drains the capacitor, so C dv/dt = −v ÷ R. Divide both sides by C, and the rule is dv/dt = −v ÷ RC. Say R = 20 kΩ and C = 100 µF. Then RC = 2 s. At 12 V the voltage falls at 6 V a second. At 6 V it falls at 3 V a second. Half the voltage gives half the rate. A coil's current, dying through a resistor once its supply is taken away, falls the same way. A sample of radioactive atoms decays exponentially too, at a rate set by their decay constant.[^2]

That proportion is why equal times take equal fractions. The rate is always the same share of the voltage. So each second takes the same share, whatever the voltage is. Here each second keeps 0.607 of the voltage, from 12 V down to 7.28 V or from 2.68 V down to 1.62 V. The flat line v = 0 is this rule's steady state. Each second keeps a fraction of what is left, so by this rule the curve closes in on it but never quite gets there.[^5] Flip the sign to dy/dt = +y ÷ τ and the same reasoning gives growth. Each equal time then multiplies the amount by the same factor.

To find the curve, [[separate the variables]]: gather every v on one side and every t on the other.[^1] Divide both sides of the rule by v, to get (1 ÷ v) dv/dt = −1 ÷ RC. It is usually written dv ÷ v = −dt ÷ RC. That is shorthand for integrating both sides over time, not for cancelling the d's. Textbooks add that the slope of ln v is 1 ÷ v, for a positive v. So integrating 1 ÷ v gives ln v. Integrating the constant −1 ÷ RC gives −t ÷ RC. Each side brings its own constant, and the two join into one + c. So ln v = −t ÷ RC + c. Raising e to a power undoes ln, so v = e^(−t/RC + c). A power of a sum splits into a product, so v = e^c × e^(−t/RC). Call e^c by one letter, A. At t = 0, e^0 = 1, so v = A. A is the start voltage, and here v = 12 e^(−t/2). Write τ for RC, and the answer is y = A e^(−t/τ). Now put it back to check. Textbooks add that the slope of e^(kt) is k times e^(kt). Here k is −1 ÷ τ, so the slope is −y ÷ τ at every t. That is the rule.

τ is the [[time constant]], and it has two readings. After each τ the amount is e^(−1), or 0.368, of what it was. A coil's current falls this way, to 0.368 of the preceding value in each time constant.[^4] The other reading comes from the starting slope, −A ÷ τ. A straight line at that slope would reach zero at exactly one τ. The curve is only down to 0.368 of its start by then. For a capacitor τ = RC, in seconds. For a coil τ = L ÷ R.[^9]

**A rate in proportion to what is left separates and integrates to y = A e^(−t/τ), with A the start and τ the time constant. In every τ it loses 0.632 of what remains.[^5]**

analogy.text: Send a signal down a long cable and each kilometre keeps the same fraction of its power. That is why a cable's loss is quoted per kilometre, in decibels. Equal lengths take equal fractions, just as equal times do here. Double the length and the fraction kept is squared, so the loss in decibels doubles.
analogy.breaks: The cable's loss runs over distance, not time, and nothing in it is stored and let go. Its loss per kilometre also changes with frequency, so a sharp pulse spreads out as it travels. A discharge has one voltage, and its curve keeps one shape.

practice.text:
**Safe way first:** by this rule a capacitor's voltage never quite reaches zero. Prove it dead with an approved tester before you touch it.

- Check the rate is in proportion to the amount. Write it as dy/dt = −y ÷ τ.
- Separate. Put every y on the left and every t on the right: dy ÷ y = −dt ÷ τ.
- Integrate both sides, with one + c: ln y = −t ÷ τ + c.
- Undo the ln: y = A e^(−t/τ).
- Use the start value. A is the amount at t = 0.
- Put it back. The slope of A e^(−t/τ) is −1 ÷ τ times itself, so both sides agree.
- Check the units. τ must come out in seconds.

**Rule of thumb:** each τ keeps 0.368 of what was there. A tangent at the starting rate reaches zero at one τ.

**Worked example:** a 470 µF capacitor at 20 V discharges through 10 kΩ. τ = RC = 10 kΩ × 470 µF = 4.7 s. So v = 20 e^(−t/4.7). Its starting rate is −20 ÷ 4.7 = −4.26 V a second. After 4.7 s it is at 20 × 0.368 = 7.36 V. After 9.4 s it is at 20 e^(−2) = 2.71 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Separating wrongly. dN = −λN dt still has N on both sides. Divide by N first.
- Leaving out the + c. Then A is 1, and the curve starts at 1 instead of at its start value.
- Turning τ upside down. y = 5 e^(−2t) has τ = 0.5 s, not 2 s.
- Reading τ as the time to empty. After one τ, 0.368 of the start is still there.
- Holding the starting rate. The rate shrinks with the amount, so the fall slows.
